content: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a gas that is colorless, odorless, tasteless, and non-irritating. It becomes toxic to humans when its concentration exceeds 100 parts per million (ppm). Causes of Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Life-Threatening Causes Life-threatening causes of carbon monoxide poisoning are those that can result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours if left untreated. Death can occur from nearly all causes of CO poisoning, depending on the levels of CO in the blood. Exposure to fire is a significant life-threatening cause. Common Causes Carbon monoxide exposure from boats or motor vehicles. Use of charcoal grills, propane stoves, or charcoal briquettes in enclosed spaces. Operation of gas-powered generators. Fires involving electrical cables. Situations immediately following hurricanes or other natural disasters. Malfunctioning or poorly maintained heating systems. Use of power washers and other gas-powered tools. Management of Acute Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Recommended Actions (Do's) Assess all possible high-risk factors and treat patients with hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy when indicated. Administer hyperbaric oxygen therapy to pregnant women regardless of the level of CO poisoning. Provide 100% oxygen therapy until the patient is symptom-free, with a minimum duration of 4–5 hours. Administer at least one hyperbaric oxygen treatment for severe cases of CO poisoning. Warn all patients about the potential for delayed neurological complications. Perform a chest X-ray in all cases of severe poisoning. Additionally, consider conducting an electrocardiogram (EKG), measuring troponin levels, and, if necessary, performing CT or MRI imaging. Schedule a follow-up visit for the patient within two weeks. Ensure the patient is isolated from the source of carbon monoxide exposure. Patients with mild symptoms may be safely discharged from the emergency department once they are symptom-free. Actions to Avoid (Don'ts) Do not rely solely on carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) levels, as they are not always reliable. Correlate findings with clinical symptoms. Do not use standard pulse oximetry, as it is not effective in detecting CO poisoning. Do not forget to perform a pregnancy test on all women of childbearing age. Do not neglect to isolate the patient from the source of carbon monoxide exposure.
